bib.title: PARSER: Read in Parallel, Reason in Depth for Long-Context LLM Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "ParSer: Read in Parallel, Reason in Depth for Long-Context LLM Agents" (printed as PARSER/ParSer). Kun Li, Zexuan Qiu, Tianhua Zhang (equal contribution), Irwin King, Helen Meng, The Chinese University of Hong Kong. arXiv:2609.06702v2 [cs.CL], 26 Sep 2026. Preprint. No venue is printed.

COVERAGE: I read about 66,500 of the 132,197 chars: the whole main text (pp. 1–11), Appendix A and B, C.1/C.2 and the start of D, plus the Agentic RAG baseline (D.3), the lead-agent tool schema and the subagent prompt. I did not read the rest of the references, the later appendix parts (D.1/D.2 details, E.4/E.6 training and inference config, Figs 5–11, F case studies) or the table-of-figures text. I searched them with grep and found no limitations section. `scripts/papers/figures.py captions` printed nothing.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: A lead agent that never sees the document, plus frozen chunk-bound subagents queried in parallel, stays flat from 7K to 896K tokens while sequential-memory agents degrade.
  number: HotpotQA average 84.57 (4B) and 86.79 (9B), against the strongest sequential baseline at 78.91 and 80.05. At 896K the 4B figure is 85.42 against 73.44.
  setup: Qwen3.5-4B and 9B lead agents, Qwen3.5-4B frozen subagents, 4,096-token chunks at inference, HotpotQA Sub_EM over 128 questions, mean of 3 runs. Baselines MemAgent and ReMemR1 were reimplemented on the same data and backbones.
  quote: "ParSer with 4B and 9B backbones achieves average accuracies of 84.6% and 86.8% respectively, outperforming the strongest sequential memory baseline by 5.7 and 6.7 percentage points; at the longest setting (896K tokens) the gaps widen to 12.0 and 9.9 percentage points"
  where: p.2, Table 1 (p.6)
- Claim: Full-context prompting loses accuracy as the document grows, even though the window is not full.
  number: Qwen3.5-4B full-context (non-think) falls from 75.78 at 7K to 34.38 at 896K. Its think mode falls from 80.47 to 31.25.
  setup: HotpotQA; YaRN RoPE scaling (factor 4) beyond 262K.
  quote: "Full-context (non-think) 75.78 75.78 71.88 74.22 67.97 61.72 53.13 34.38 64.36"
  where: Table 1, p.6
- Claim: A 9B ParSer beats a 1M-context frontier model.
  number: +6.3 points over DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Its HotpotQA average is 80.47 in think-max mode and 75.10 in non-think. At 896K, non-think scores 62.50 and think-max 78.91.
  setup: DeepSeek-V4-Pro preview of 2026-04-24, reasoning effort Max, HotpotQA.
  quote: "Scaling to a 9B backbone, ParSer achieves an average of 86.8%, surpassing DeepSeek-V4-Pro ... by 6.3 percentage points."
  where: p.2, Table 1
- Claim: Sequential memory agents are sensitive to where evidence sits, to the order of evidence and to the distance between pieces. ParSer is not.
  number: Reversing the evidence order drops MemAgent and ReMemR1 sharply. In the Fig. 2(b) extraction the values are 66.5, 75.5 and 96.4 for the logical order and 23.3, 61.7 and 97.1 for the reversed order, in the order MemAgent, ReMemR1, ParSer (my reading of the figure labels). Across distance buckets ParSer holds 87.1–88.7, while ReMemR1 falls from 77.2 to 61.0 and MemAgent sits at 44–50 (Fig. 2c).
  setup: 512 questions per control, 894K-token documents, Qwen3.5-4B. Order and distance controls use 2WikiMultiHopQA; the position control uses HotpotQA.
  quote: "Both MemAgent and ReMemR1 suffer a sharp performance drop when the order is reversed, whereas ParSer remains stable."
  where: §4.1, p.7, Fig. 2
- Claim: Parallel reading cuts wall-clock latency, but the advantage shrinks as concurrency rises.
  number: At 896K and concurrency 1, MemAgent takes 876.20s per sample against 78.22s for ParSer (about 11×). At concurrency 16 it is 101.94s against 58.86s (1.7×). At concurrency 32 it is 74.96s against 58.76s.
  setup: Amortized time per sample over 128 samples, SGLang. ParSer uses two GPUs (an H100 for the subagents, an RTX3090 for the lead agent); the baselines use one H100. Full-context fails at 896K under concurrency.
  quote: "parallel reading yields an 11× reduction at 896K tokens under single concurrency (876s vs. 78s per sample relative to MemAgent) and maintains a 1.7× advantage under a concurrency of 16 (102s vs. 59s)."
  where: p.2, Table 2 (p.8)
- Claim: The sequential step count grows with document length for MemAgent but stays near the number of reasoning hops for ParSer.
  number: ParSer takes about 4 lead-agent rounds at every length (3.9–4.13). MemAgent grows to 183.58 steps at 896K.
  setup: HotpotQA, same questions at all lengths.
  quote: "ParSer processes document chunks in parallel, reducing the number of sequential inference steps to the number of reasoning hops required to solve the question itself."
  where: §4.2 and Fig. 3, p.9
- Claim: Chunking and short per-subagent context drive the gain. A single subagent fed the full document loses most of it.
  number: Chunk 4096 averages 84.57. Full document averages 73.76 and drops to 53.13 at 896K. Chunk sizes 16K, 64K and 131K average 83.59, 81.84 and 80.34.
  setup: Qwen3.5-4B, HotpotQA, YaRN beyond the native window for the Full setting.
  quote: "Table 4 reports a notable performance drop upon the removal of chunking, particularly on long-document subsets."
  where: §4.3, Table 4, p.9
- Claim: Subagent size saturates at 4B. The lead agent also works with thinking subagents and with DCI (grep/rg shell-tool) subagents without retraining.
  number: Subagent 2B averages 78.26, 4B 84.57 and 9B 84.77. DCI standalone averages 75.61, lead + DCI 84.67, lead + thinking 85.55.
  setup: Lead agent fixed at Qwen3.5-4B, HotpotQA.
  quote: "performance improves when replacing the 2B subagent with the 4B version, and then saturates when employing an even larger subagent (9B)."
  where: Tables 3 and 5, pp.9–10
- Claim: Subagent output is sparse, which keeps the lead agent's context small and cuts decoding cost.
  number: Total output tokens at 896K are 187,058 for MemAgent against 541+804 (lead + subagents) for ParSer. The decode-computation ratio falls from 13.9% at 7K to 0.4% at 896K.
  setup: Qwen3.5-4B, theoretical formula with n/T=5000 and K=4, assuming enough GPU memory to keep every chunk's KV cache.
  quote: "MemAgent produces a memory of about 1K tokens for every chunk, whereas each ParSer subagent emits only a short finding or an 'Unknown' response for its chunk"
  where: Appendix A, Table 6, p.15–16
- Claim: RL on the lead agent adds about 10 points, and the untrained workflow already beats both trained memory baselines.
  number: HotpotQA 4B average goes from 74.42 to 84.57. MemAgent without RL scores 45.05 and ReMemR1 without RL 45.67.
  setup: GRPO with binary exact-match reward, 32,768 synthetic HotpotQA samples of about 28K tokens, K≤9 in training and 12 at inference, observation tokens masked from the loss.
  quote: "average HotpotQA accuracy rises from 74.42 to 84.57 on Qwen3.5-4B and from 76.24 to 86.79 on Qwen3.5-9B"
  where: Appendix B.1, p.16
- Claim: ParSer carries over to non-QA RULER tasks.
  number: Mostly 97–100 on needle-in-a-haystack. Variable Tracking ranges 90.9–99.1 for the 4B lead agent.
  setup: Ten RULER tasks, 8K–512K tokens, 8,192-token chunks.
  where: Appendix B.2, Fig. 4, p.18
- Claim: The architecture exists to keep the workers' tokens out of the leader's context.
  number: none
  quote: "a leader dispatching subtasks to workers that each run in an isolated context window is by now a common pattern in agentic systems (Anthropic, 2025), since a worker's intermediate tokens never occupy the leader's context."
  where: §5.2, p.11

LIMITS
- Every task is multi-hop QA over synthetic haystacks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA padded with distractor Wikipedia paragraphs) plus synthetic RULER. There is no agentic, code or real-document workload.
- Each test uses 128 questions reused across all eight lengths. No variance or significance figures are given beyond "average over 3 runs".
- The latency comparison is not like-for-like on hardware: ParSer gets two GPUs, and the subagents also use 10 extra H100s during training.
- The authors concede the advantage shrinks at high concurrency. If chunk KV caches are evicted, prefill cost rises from O(n²/T) to O(Kn²/T), about 4× MemAgent's at K=4.
- Training uses 512-token chunks and inference uses 4,096. The authors say they chose this to train faster, which leaves a mismatch.
- Table 1 shows "-" for every Agentic RAG cell, so that baseline is described in §3.2 and D.3 but has no reported numbers in this extraction.
- No limitations section was found in the pages I read.
- Models and baselines are dated to 2026 and use the Qwen3.5 backbones and a preview of DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

BUILDS ON: MemAgent (Yu et al., 2026), whose data recipe and test sets it reuses. ReMemR1 (Shi et al., 2026). GRU-Mem (Sheng et al., 2026). ReAct (Yao et al., 2023). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and RLVR (DeepSeek-AI, 2025a). Context rot (Hong et al., 2025) and "lost in the middle" (Liu et al., 2024). LLM×MapReduce (Zhou et al., 2024). LongAgent (Zhao et al., 2024). Chain-of-Agents (Zhang et al., 2024). Anthropic's multi-agent research system post (2025). Agentic RAG (Jin et al., 2025). DCI (Li et al., 2026). SGLang, VERL and YaRN.

CODE: Lead-agent tool schema (Appendix E.1, p.21): `"name": "query_agents", "description": "Broadcast a query to all document agents in parallel. Each agent reads only its chunk and may return evidence and a partial answer. The tool response is a JSON string of aggregated findings."`

Subagent output contract (E.2, p.22): "Binary Output: Either provide JSON with evidence, or output exactly Unknown." The JSON has `{"evidence": "Exact verbatim quote from the chunk...", "answer": "..."}`. Abstentions are dropped before the result enters the lead agent's context.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.3): sequential chain of T dependent memory updates against K scatter–gather rounds. It shows the architecture fastest.
- Fig 2 (p.7): accuracy under controlled evidence position, order and distance. This is the main evidence of robustness.
- Fig 3 (p.9): step counts, with MemAgent growing and ParSer flat at about 4.
- Tables 1, 2 and 4 hold the central numbers.

PROBLEMS
- Figure captions could not be extracted with the script, so I took figure facts from the text. Fig. 2(b) values are my reading of the extracted labels.
- No embedded instructions in the PDF. The system-prompt text in Appendix E is paper content, not directed at me.
- Table 1 has some garbled spacing, and the Agentic RAG rows are blank.

FIT FOR THE COURSE
- It is a long-context reading paper, not a tool-design paper. It is on topic for context engineering, but it does not address tool-output formatting or tool-schema design.
- Best fit in note 10 (tools and multi-agent): the section on isolating subagent context, i.e. sub-agents return condensed findings and abstentions are dropped. It supports "tool or worker outputs should be small, structured and filtered before entering the lead's window", and the JSON-or-Unknown contract is a concrete example.
- Secondary fit: note 05 (compression and compaction) as a counterexample to recurrent memory compression. Note 11 (failure modes) can take the context-rot and position-sensitivity numbers. Note 04 (retrieval) is a weak fit, since the Agentic RAG numbers are missing.
- Quality: a solid preprint with consistent ablations. Its generality is limited to synthetic multi-hop QA, from one lab, with latency claims that depend on the hardware.
